blocks.text: "Between you and I, the arrangement was unfair." That sentence is spoken every day in Nigerian offices and it is wrong every time. One small word — the case of a pronoun — is the difference, and examiners test it in almost every Lexis and Structure paper.

blocks.markdown:
A **pronoun** stands in for a noun so that we do not have to repeat it. Instead of "Amina said Amina would bring Amina's textbook", we say "Amina said she would bring her textbook".

The noun a pronoun replaces is called its **antecedent**. Almost every pronoun error in an exam comes from one of two failures: choosing the wrong **case**, or failing to agree with the **antecedent**.

blocks.title: Case
blocks.text: The form a pronoun takes according to its job. Subjective case for subjects and complements (I, he, she, we, they, who); objective case for objects and after prepositions (me, him, her, us, them, whom); possessive case for ownership (my, his, her, our, their, whose).

blocks.markdown:
### The three rules that earn the marks

**1. After a preposition, always use the objective case.**
*Between you and **me***. *This is a secret among **us** three*. *She sat beside **him** and **me***.

**2. Test a compound subject or object by removing the other person.**
"The principal praised Ade and (I / me)." Remove *Ade and*: you would never say "The principal praised I", so it must be **me**.

**3. After *than* and *as*, restore the missing verb.**
"My brother is taller than (I / me)." Restore the verb: "taller than **I** am". So formal English requires **I**.

blocks.title: Choosing between *who* and *whom*
blocks.prompt: Complete the sentence: "The candidate ______ the panel recommended has been offered the post."

steps.text: Isolate the relative clause on its own: '______ the panel recommended'.
Rearrange it into normal statement order: 'the panel recommended ______'.
Substitute an ordinary personal pronoun. You would say 'the panel recommended him', not 'the panel recommended he'.
*Him* is objective, and the objective form of *who* is *whom*.
Read the whole sentence back to confirm it sounds right: 'The candidate whom the panel recommended has been offered the post.'

blocks.answer: whom — because the pronoun is the object of *recommended*, and the *him* test confirms the objective case

blocks.markdown:
### Agreement with the antecedent

A pronoun must match its antecedent in **number**, **person** and **gender**. The trap is a plural noun sitting between the real antecedent and the pronoun:

- *Each of the girls has **her** own lamp.* — the antecedent is *Each*, not *girls*.
- *Neither of the boys has done **his** work.* — the antecedent is *Neither*.
- *Everybody must sign **his or her** name.* — indefinite pronouns ending in -body and -one are singular.

Ignore any phrase beginning with *of*, *with*, *as well as* or *together with* when you look for the antecedent.

blocks.title: Reflexives are not polite subjects
blocks.text: "Myself and my brother travelled to Jos" is wrong. A reflexive pronoun can never be a subject. Write "My brother and I travelled to Jos". Use *myself* only when the subject acts on itself: "I hurt myself."

blocks.title: The removal test
blocks.text: Whenever two names or pronouns are joined by *and*, cover one of them and read the sentence again. Your ear will almost always pick the right case once the second item is out of the way. This single trick answers most pronoun questions in WAEC and JAMB.

points: A pronoun replaces a noun; the noun it replaces is its antecedent.
Subjects and complements take the subjective case; objects and words after prepositions take the objective case.
Remove the other item from a compound to hear which case is correct.
After *than* and *as*, restore the understood verb to decide the case.
A pronoun agrees with its true antecedent, not with a plural noun sitting in an intervening *of* phrase.
Reflexive pronouns never act as subjects.
